Turf inside ChampionsGate's screened pool cages and lanais

Pool and lanai turf in ChampionsGate prices in the $8–$18 per sq ft range as of September 2026. Screened pool cages are close to standard on the resort-style homes built across both the Osceola and Polk sides of the community, and the strip of ground inside that screen is often the one part of the yard sod never held onto in the first place.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Screened cages are the norm on ChampionsGate's resort-built homes

A private pool inside a screen enclosure is close to the default layout on the vacation-home construction that fills ChampionsGate's resort district and townhome rows, and the same style shows up plenty in the gated owner-occupied villages too. The ground inside that screen gets shade from the cage frame for part of the day and heavy foot traffic in wet swimsuits the rest of it, a combination sod handles poorly and turf handles by design, since it doesn't need sun to survive and doesn't hold water the way soil does underfoot. Our note on turf and melting risk near reflective glass is worth a read before placing turf close to a low-E slider, and the pool and lanai turf guide covers deck-mounted installs beyond ChampionsGate.

What does a small deck border cost, worked out?

Installed turf runs eight to eighteen dollars a square foot, typically ten to sixteen, and price does not change by ChampionsGate ZIP code, only by access, base condition, and drainage. Say a homeowner wants a 250 sq ft strip between the pool cage and a side fence turfed rather than reseeded: at the typical range, that job runs somewhere between roughly twenty-five hundred and four thousand dollars, before accounting for anything unusual about the site. A quote well outside that range for a plain open border, high or low, is worth asking about specifically, since the underlying material and labor do not vary by neighborhood.

Say you have a 400 sq ft pool deck

Say you have a 400 sq ft strip of concrete pool deck inside a screen cage on a rental villa in ChampionsGate's resort district, currently bare and hot underfoot by afternoon. At the $8–$18 per sq ft range, glue-down turf over that deck runs $3,200 to $7,200, with the underlay and edge work usually pushing a small enclosed area like this toward the top of the band rather than the bottom. Scheduling the two-day job between guest stays is the main coordination point, since the deck has to be fully cured before the next check-in, and a property manager with a booking calendar handles that timing better than picking a date and hoping it holds.

Turf over the pool deck itself, not just around it

Where the deck is concrete rather than pavers, which is common inside these cages, turf goes down with a drainage underlay and glue-down edges rather than the nailed perimeter a lawn gets, since there's no soil underneath to anchor into. That underlay is what keeps water from sheeting across the deck after a rinse or a rain instead of passing through, and it's a different install method entirely from a backyard conversion even though the finished look reads the same to a guest walking out to the pool.

Why a slab that never fully dries is a warning sign

A glued lanai floor built without enough drainage underlay traps splash and rinse water against the concrete instead of routing it to the deck drain, and the first sign is usually a slab that stays damp longer after use than it should, not a visible puddle anyone notices right away in ChampionsGate's humidity. Adhesive bonds weaker against a slab that never fully dries between uses, so a corner that lifts months after installation often traces back to that trapped moisture rather than a bad glue job on its own. Fixing it after the fact means pulling turf, not just adding infill.

Grading a deck border toward the drain it already has

Most yards only need their base graded one to two percent away from the house, but a pool-deck border in ChampionsGate gets aimed at the deck's existing low point instead, since runoff already sheds off the cage and coping onto that strip during every storm. Washed, open-graded crushed rock underneath keeps that added flow moving rather than binding into a crust at the transition where concrete meets soil. Skipping this and grading only away from the foundation leaves water pooling along the coping edge, which is exactly where bare feet cross most often on the way in and out of a ChampionsGate cage.

What a nightly-rental pool cage needs that an owner-occupied one doesn't

A rental villa's pool area sees a new set of feet, sunscreen and pool chemicals every week or two, and a property manager scheduling turnover cleaning benefits from a surface that rinses clean fast between groups rather than one that needs raking or edging. An owner-occupied pool cage in a gated village gets the same turf but a slower wear cycle, since it's one household's routine rather than a rotating guest list putting the surface through its paces.

Converting an existing bare or gravel pool border to turf

Replacing bare dirt or loose gravel along an existing ChampionsGate pool deck with turf starts by removing that old material and confirming the grade underneath still falls the one to two percent it should toward the deck's existing drain, since gravel borders in particular are sometimes laid flatter than the water actually needs to move correctly. Only after that grade is confirmed or corrected does the washed rock base go in, followed by the same seaming and anchoring any pool-border turf job uses. Skipping the grade check because there was already something there is how an old drainage problem gets buried under a new surface instead of fixed.

What two years of splash and chemical exposure does to a border

Turf directly bordering a ChampionsGate pool takes more chemical exposure, chlorine or salt splash, over two years than turf anywhere else on the property, which makes a second-year check of that specific stretch worth doing separately from a general perimeter walk. Comparing infill depth and backing condition in the immediate splash zone against a section of the same border further from the water shows whether that exposure is aging one part of the job faster than the rest. A splash zone holding up the same as the rest of the border after two years is a good sign the original build and rinse routine are both working.

Questions people ask

Does turf over a pool deck need the same base as a lawn?

No. A concrete deck inside a screen cage gets a drainage underlay and glued, taped seams instead of the washed crushed-rock base and nailed edges a soil lawn needs, since there's no ground to build up underneath it.

Do property managers usually schedule pool-area turf between guest bookings?

Yes, that's the common pattern in ChampionsGate's rental villages, and it's worth telling us the booking calendar up front so the job doesn't overlap a check-in.
